description: We are space beth and we are here to rock
summary: Lookout is a browser game where one to four players design, launch and fly an Earth-observation satellite that spots wildfires or maps air quality. From a 3D mission-control cockpit, four roles (Science Lead, Mission Architect, Systems Engineer and Operations Lead) make twelve linked decisions, watching mass, power, battery, data, budget, science and confidence margins move before they commit. The design earns its launch odds; then six fortnights of operations draw mission cards from the design's own weak spots. A tested orbital-mechanics engine computes the real orbit behind every turn: eclipses, ground-station passes, orbit drift, drag and the de-orbit burn. Progress is measured with JPL's Concept Maturity Levels, and the final report shows which decision caused each outcome, so players learn why missions succeed or fail.
details:
Full walkthrough at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=duUk94cvBhw

What it does. Lookout turns the NASA challenge's trade-offs into decisions you can feel. Players sit in a mission-control cockpit: a curved wall of screens around a 3D view of their spacecraft, its orbit, its ground stations or its rocket. The mission runs in four phases.

  1. Build. Twelve decisions across four roles: what to observe, which instrument, the duty cycle, the orbit, the launcher, the architecture, the spacecraft bus, the battery plan, the mass reserve, the ground stations, the data plan and the contingency. Each card previews its effect on every margin, a margin turns yellow under 25 % (NASA Goddard's early-design margin, GSFC-STD-1000) and red over the limit, and stressors such as a slipping rideshare interrupt with a timer.
  2. Launch. Go / no-go only when every limit closes. Launch odds come from the design (margins, maturity, studies); players can launch now or pay to hold for a better window.
  3. Orbit. Six fortnights of operations. Each draws a bonus or malus card shaped by the design, such as a drag surge for a low orbit or a ground-station outage for a single station, and the team can pay to prepare for the forecast card.
  4. Report. A score out of 100 (science returned, mission health, engineering process, efficiency), the weakest area, and a mission log that names the decision behind every event.

How it works. Three layers, all TypeScript: an orbital-mechanics engine (Kepler propagation, J2 drift, sun-synchronous orbits, eclipse geometry, ground-station visibility, atmospheric drag, Hohmann and Lambert transfers, CR3BP) with unit tests; pure, seeded game rules on top, so a mission can be replayed exactly and 200 simulated players can test the balance in under a second; and a three.js cockpit that draws the same numbers the rules use. Every figure in the game data (instruments, launchers and prices, ground stations, costs, the $37M budget cap) cites its source in the repository.

Benefits. Students learn systems thinking by doing: every number has a cause, and changing one decision visibly moves the others. Simulated play shows that good decisions win and luck alone doesn't: random play averages 62/100, careful play with studies 89/100. A built-in handbook explains every concept from the decision that uses it.

Accessibility. Every control works by keyboard with a visible focus ring, screen readers get a text description of the 3D view and live announcements, text contrast is at least 4.5:1, gains and losses never rely on colour alone, reduced-motion settings are respected, and a flat view presents the same game as a plain page.

Tools. TypeScript, Bun, Vite, React, shadcn/ui, Tailwind CSS, three.js and Biome, hosted on Cloudflare Workers. No AI-generated images, video or audio in the game.

Next. Online team rooms (each role on its own device), and a ladder of new scenarios reusing the engine: a Moon transfer, Mars launch windows and a telescope at L2.

Honest limits. Science is scored in game units rather than sourced revisit and resolution requirements; a few figures have no public source and are labelled n/a; team play is pass-and-play on one screen for now.
